entry.title: Waxing poetic about my records and turntable
entry.summary: My thoughts on collecting and playing vinyl records.
entry.content:
Music in the streaming age is weightless. It reaches you through the aether from servers thousands of miles away into whatever speaker happens to be nearby. It seems almost infinite, is completely free of friction, and incredibly easy to take for granted.

I recently bought a record player and my first three records, with plans to buy more.

To anyone used to tapping a glass screen to hear any song ever recorded, this looks like too much work to listen to a limited number of tunes. Records are bulky, inconvenient, require physical storage, and only hold about twenty minutes of music per side before you have to get up and flip them over.

Yet, much like taking the time to manually grind whole coffee beans instead of stirring instant powder into boiling water, the friction adds to its appeal.

The instant coffee vs. freshly brewed coffee analogy breaks down when it comes to quality though. Any coffee connoisseur will say brewed coffee tastes better than instant (due to a variety of reasons), but standard CD-quality digital audio technically has higher fidelity and dynamic range than vinyl ever will. Records degrade over time due to dust and scratches, leading to sound artifacts (which I am coming to terms with), and cost a ridiculous amount of money in India, thanks to import duties and a weak rupee.

What makes a record “worth it”, still

I’m sort of a minimalist and never thought I’d have a collection of anything, but I love music and hate how exploitative streaming is (more on this later), so it makes complete sense to have a little record collection.

Here are some reasons I started one, in no particular order.

Difference from digital media

Unlike digital files which store sound as a collection of bits, a vinyl record is a direct physical artifact of audio.

When a record is pressed, soundwaves are literally etched into a single continuous groove on a sheet of PVC plastic. If you zoomed in with a microscope, you'd see the actual undulating shape of the soundwaves themselves.

It’s such a delicate, magical, yet simple thing, and it boggles my mind that this exists at all.

Relative rarity

Vinyl records went out of fashion because of their cost of production, fragility, and low portability, and everyone streams, so it makes the experience even more interesting, as I didn’t get to listen to any until recently. You did however see them in all sorts of media, especially that from the heyday of records, which added to the mystique.

The art looks really pretty

The sleeve, of course, has the album art, which is usually pretty enough on its own, but they also quite commonly have things like lyrics booklets,

Records themselves look good as well

Our first record, ali by Vieux Farka Touré and Khruangbin, was a translucent blue-green instead of the usual black, which was such a pleasant surprise.

Another record I purchased, “Is This It” by The Strokes, is a limited editiion translucent red.

Plain black records also look great, though.

You might enjoy the music more

The ritual of pulling the disc from its sleeve, cleaning off the dust, gently lowering the tonearm, and watching it spin anchors your attention to the room. It turns listening into a dedicated activity rather than background noise.

Dust and cat hair gets on the record, which causes pop sounds, so one has to clean it, and the act of moving it to and from the sleeves and the turntable creates static, which makes a sort of buzzing sound. You really have to love a record to want to go through all of that. It connects you to the activity of listening instead of being a passive participant, and I guess the work makes you appreciate it more?

Streaming pays very little

The artist gets more money. If you buy a record in India, maybe 10% of the sale price has actually gone to the artist (because the retailer, the government, the publisher, etc all take their cut), but it takes 100,000 to 150,000 streams on Spotify for an artist to net the same amount. Streaming is hell for smaller artists especially, and is not enough to make a living.

A section of Wikipedia on Spotify’s compensation practices

More miscellaneous reasons

  • My partner’s cousins and brother have one.
  • It’s a physical display of your music tastes.
  • Actually owning your music.
  • Records and the turntable and other equipment look really good in a room, and you can talk about it.

Neighbourhood record store

I live quite close to this cute record store called On the jungle floor. They’ve got a massive collection of records and the staff is friendly. I love visiting there to just look at the really expensive equipment they have and drool at the LPs they have.

Two of the records we’ve bought have been from here!

An interesting thing I heard after a couple of conversations there with people either working or hanging out there as friends of the owner, people volunteer there for free for some reason? Not sure why anyone would do that other than as a favour to a friend. If any reader has done something like this for a for-profit business, please let me know.

There was a guy behind the counter who wasn’t an empployee. He’s a DJ and was playing some of his personal records from a massive tote bag full of records, trying to figure out what to play on his next set. Maybe he was getting the most out of the ₹3L turntable. I didn’t get to talk to him too much, but my partner really liked the LPs he had, and since we can’t find them for sale anywhere in India, this has caused a lot of consternation. For anyone who want to check out his music, his name is Saksham, @ghewxr on Instagram.

The current rig

I’m using an almost entry-level turntable from

I just use a portable bluetooth speaker via aux at the moment because dumping all my disposable income into a new hobby would be silly. Even when I do get speakers, I’m going for the (relatively) cheaper end for now. I’m not an audiophile, and thank god for that. Like every hobby there’s a way to dump all your money into this. After a certain point, you get diminishing returns and are just trying to optimise the fun out of your equipment.

I’m thinking of doing listening parties, though, and the idea of bringing people over to listen to music coming out of a cheap portable speaker does seem a bit sad. Down the line, the goal is to set up a proper stereo amplifier connected to a decent pair of passive bookshelf speakers, giving the physical media room to actually push some air. The bass on the Strokes album goes hard, so a subwoofer is also on the cards.

Thinking of getting Polk Audio Monitor XT15 Compact Bookshelf Speaker from avstore.in alongside the Fosi Audio V3 amplifier. This will go great with my hiby music player as well, letting me listen to digital music from a more “intentional” source than streaming.

entry.title: Getting into craft coffee
entry.summary: Explaining why I drink my coffee black and what I like about it
entry.content:
Thank you @zyd for the request, and IndieWebClub Bangalore for the prompt that sort-of points to it.

You probably don’t need coffee explained to you. It’s the most popular drug delivery mechanism in the world, and could be considered the lifeblood of modern civilisation (or at least jobs-oriented capitalism). That is to say, you might consume, or be surrounded by people who consume the liquid. Most people use it just as a way to receive the alertness that comes with ingesting caffeine. It can also add a sort of roast-y and rich flavour to popular food items like your tiramisus, affogatos, and caramel macchiatos. I also like coffee a lot (check out my domain drew.coffee if you’re not reading this over there), but without any adornments like milk, sweeteners, or additional flavour. This does cause a bit of surprise to anyone visiting my home or hanging out at a café with me, due to the assumption that coffee on its own tastes pretty bad, which in turn still surprises me a little.

Coffee is a beverage brewed from roasted and ground coffee beans, coffee beans being the seed of the Coffea plants. They’re not actually beans, since they’re not a legume, but the point is they come from a fruit. Coffee thus actually has a quite fruity flavour when not roasted too darkly (and even then you can taste a hint), along with an assortment of other flavours due to the content of the soil, how the plant was grown, the altitude, and so on.

Why you think coffee tastes like charcoal on its own

The reason why most people associate coffee with a stronger roast and the distinct flavour that comes with it is because:

  • Strongly roasted beans last a smidge longer without going bad
  • The fruity and aromatic flavours of a lighter roast go away much quicker when stored
  • When you’re selling coffee at a large-scale business like starbucks, you want your base ingredient to taste consistent, and a strong roast burns away all the uniqueness of the seeds, and you just taste the roast.
  • People assume a stronger roasted coffee contains more caffeine (the opposite is true)
  • It tastes better with milk drinks, since the flavour cuts through the milk and other things one might add to the drink.
  • Darker roasted beans are easier to work with for espressos, which are the most popular drink base in cafés.

Craft (or specialty) coffee

Ever heard a sommelier talk about wine? Each estate and vintage is supposed to have its own unique characteristics which you can taste (though the jury’s out on whether sommeliers are faking it for attention). They taste different because they were grown on different soil and atmospheric conditions, and processed a bit differently after harvest. The same applies to coffee. When you treat the coffee itself as the end-goal and not a necessary evil you need to get your dose of stimulants, there’s a lot which you can play with. You can taste the intrinsic flavours of the bean itself (though this is a bit subtle), the way in which it was prepared for roasting (some methods aim to clear as much fruit as effectively as possible, leading to a clearer coffee flavour, while others ferment with the skin on or media like honey), and even aging. There’s a world of experiences when consuming coffee this way, and you could go your whole life without tasting every possible method. And after you get a bit accustomed to it, you will be able to taste the flavour notes of each bag or cup of coffee you get from a specialty coffee shop. Those are usually noted on the menu, such as various fruits, chocolate, and other yummy things. If you’re used to dark-roasted coffee this might seem like a bit of hogwash, but it’s real.

How to get into it

The first order of business is to figure out whether you even like coffee on its own. There’s no shame in it if you don’t. Look up specialty coffee + your city/neighbourhood in your search engine of choice, and go to the friendly barista and tell them you’d like to try a manual pour. Maybe you can talk to them and figure out what exactly you’re looking for. If you have a friend who’s into specialty coffee, that’s perfect because they’re probably going to froth at their mouth when faced with the idea of inducting someone else into the hobby. If you don’t like it, and you trust that the person who prepared it did not screw up, you may stop.

The rest of this post is a short description of how you can make specialty coffee, but Hiran has a wonderful in-depth post on the same topic that might suit you better and help you decide things. Coffee Brewing 101 by Hiran

If you want to brew coffee at home, there’s not much in the way of requirements! You just need:

  • Coffee grounds
  • A way to heat water
  • A way to filter out the grounds when brewed.

You can get pre-ground coffee anywhere, just look for a lighter roast ground a bit course if all you have is a sieve (otherwise you’ll get grounds in the end product; not the best accouterment). Once you decide you like coffee enough to invest in making it at home, here’s the equipment you’ll be happy you have:

  • A conical-burr grinder. Pre-ground coffee is good, but this is fresher. It's a tiny bit pricier than a blade grinder, but grinds the coffee more evenly, meaning the pieces all brew at the same rate. Otherwise you might get the coffee a bit sour at spots, and bitter at others.
  • A coffee maker like a french press.
  • A scale to figure out what ratio of coffee to water you enjoy (there are recommendations, but your taste is unique).

Good luck, and send me an email if you try specialty coffee.

entry.title: Rules for making a playlist
entry.summary: Some guidelines I try to follow when making a playlist for others.
entry.content:
Curating a collection of music for a loved one to listen to is a time-honoured tradition, becoming accessible and a huge part of pop culture around the time cassette tapes and home-recording became possible. With the rise of music streaming, we mostly make playlists on Deezer or whatever now, sending a link to it instead of transferring a physical object. I deeply enjoy making playlists, so I’ve had a lot of time to think about what I think about when I make one.

Jacek Halicki, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

I got new rules I count 'em

  • Only one song per artist. I have favourites sometimes, and this prevents me from just stuffing the playlist with their songs.
  • It either has a specific mood: that is, it tries to evoke a certain emotion. If it is intended to switch between emotions, the shifts should be gradual and smooth.
  • Medium length, between 20 to 45 minutes. I want the recipient to be able to listen to it all at once, and feel satisfied if they do.

These rules are obviously not concrete. You can (and I do) break them for effect. A short playlist could be used to convey something really specific. A long playlist could be used to portray a more general mood, or just act as a soundtrack to some other task (e.g. for a road-trip). Artist-specific playlists can obviously exist, as a sort of Greatest Hits compilation.

A playlist

I've lost a bunch of playlists I made on a certain streaming platform once I migrated off it, but I made one recently for my beau. I was quite sleepy at around 1 am on a school night, so it might not exactly be a work of art, but I'd just like to immortalise it in a way outside of a proprietary service. This also contains a bunch of my favourite songs (though I guess all playlists I make would?)

  2. Men I Trust - "Sugar"

  4. Charli xcx - "Camera"

  5. Lorde - "What Was That"

entry.title: Why it took me a while to go vegan
entry.summary: An exploration of the personal biases, cultural baggage, and moral perfectionism that delayed my switch to veganism, and how I finally made the shift.
entry.content:
The reasons to become vegan are well-known, (here are some reasons to go vegan), and it’s not as hard to go vegan as one would think. This post is specifically about why I never went vegan earlier than when I actually did.

Reasons for me to not go vegan

  • I did not grow up in a vegetarian family, and the inherent casteism of Indian vegetarianism[1] (it’s mostly about ritual purity rather than actual care for animals, since they’d be vegan otherwise) alienated me from vegetarianism, and by extension, veganism.
  • If you start thinking about minimising suffering from a utilitarian perspective, there is almost nothing you can do to not be involved in it, at least indirectly. There is intense slavery in the globalised supply chain[2], for example, and if one wished to clean their hands of everything wrong with the world, there’s not much they could participate in.
  • I always thought people positioning veganism as the only moral option was unfair on indigenous people who live(d) sustainably as part of their surroundings, rather than engaging in destructive practices.
  • I thought PETA was annoying.
  • I used to live with someone who ate a lot of chicken, and could not be arsed to cook a separate meal for myself.
  • I had trouble eating vegetables when I was younger. This might be because I hated the way they were cooked at home.
  • Vegan food is still niche in India where even though there’s a sizeable vegetarian population, dairy is everywhere. I believe if you tell the average Indian you don’t consume dairy they’re going to think you’re crazy.
  • I felt people would no longer take me seriously if I told them I was vegan.

My current thoughts

Being vegan for me is specifically about not being complicit in unnecessary animal deaths. It is okay to decide what I wish to eat on my short life on this planet. I don’t want to eat animals and I don’t want them to be grown for food, when perfectly serviceable alternatives exist. I don’t have to participate in this just to prove some sort of point to myself. I no longer feel like have to solve all the issues in the world to care about this one thing.

entry.title: What I would do if I was invisible for a day
entry.summary: Article based on a prompt. Suggestions welcome.
entry.content:
This prompt comes from IndieWebClub Bangalore. I have had 25 minutes to pen this down.

Frankly, logistics are the main constraint. I would hate to spend my period of invisibility on an airplane flying to a different country in order to optimise my experience, but thankfully there is much to do within the bounds of Bangalore.

Something that would be very tempting to do is go somewhere with a high density of valuable goods and start stealing stuff, but I don’t reckon the prompt was about how to extract the maximum economic benefit from my condition.

If highly illegal stuff (like say, breaking into a corrupt individual’s home in order to reveal their crimes, not that I would ever consider it in any other non-hypothetical situation) is off the table, I might go to a library, as schlocky as that may sound. I haven’t been to a proper, huge library since my university days, and would love to just go around looking at all the books available and noting down what interests me. The way one finds out what to read without a library is this neat trick called “asking people”, but I have not gotten many suggestions yet. If you’re reading this, email me book suggestions.

I am frankly ashamed of how little of an id I seem to have. I would go around petting dogs (who would not be alarmed since they’d be able to smell me), sampling small bits of food and drink from bakeries, and try to execute skateboarding tricks on some smooth paved road in someone’s private estate. I don’t know any skateboarding tricks other than pumping, but have been meaning to learn, so it’d be a great time to follow through without the fear of seeming silly and having access to a nice, smooth surface (a luxury within India).

Speaking of estates, I’m sure the super rich have some really cool artwork hidden in their homes that only their rich friends get to see. It would be hard to triage which ones to hit and in which order, but perhaps there’s a list out there of Bangalore millionaires with great taste. Magazines and e-papers thrive on such trite articles.

If there were any league football games on in the area I’d take the opportunity to get close to the field and experience the game in a way that’s hard to do from the stands or the screen. Maybe run around behind the referee.

I think the theme is I would like to partake in situations I would normally not be allowed to get close to in my civilian life? Here is where a lack of desire stymies me. I can play Persona on my switch in my home without being invisible and that’s what I’ve been feeling like doing the most lately anyway.

entry.title: Git config for multiple accounts
entry.summary: Snippets of useful git configurations (when you have multiple identities)
entry.content:
I use git, as the version control system both at my workplace and to store my personal code (including the source of this blog).

I use different e-mails for personal and work repositories, as well as different SSH keys for different accounts (this is because Github, at least, does not allow different accounts to use the same key, which I was not sure of, but Ariel confirmed on fedi).

After a bunch of trial-and-error, I have figured out a way to do ssh for two different github accounts using different keys on the same device. The .sshconfig looks a bit like this:

Host work
  User git
  HostName github.com
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_work_github

Host personal
  User git
  HostName github.com
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_personal_github

So, if I want to clone a work repo, I need to do git clone work:<WorkOrg>/<RepoName>.git, and if I want to do the same using my personal account, git clone personal:<Org>/<RepoName>.git, and it just works.

I have to remember to use the correct prefix, work or personal, and if I use the wrong one, I get an error saying I can’t access the repository. To do this, I either have to change the original clone url copied from the forge, which would be something like git@github.com:<Org>/<RepoName>.git, or type the whole thing out.

Turns out, git allows one to use text substution for URLs, which fixes the problem!

[url "work:<WorkOrg>/"]
    insteadOf = https://github.com/<WorkOrg>/
    insteadOf = ssh://git@github.com/<WorkOrg>/

[url "personal"]
    insteadOf = https://github.com
    insteadOf = ssh://git@github.com

git substitutes using the longest matching URL, so if the repository is under the work Org, it will use the first rule, and otherwise use my personal key+account.

This is not the only problem though. Git forges do not use the ssh key (or your username+password) to identify the committer, but rather the email address and name set in your git config. Yes, this means anyone can spoof your identity on their commits (which is why we have signed commits). How you fix this, is you run the following commands per repository if you are using a different name and email than the ones you have set globally:

git config set user.name "Drew Jose"
git config set user.email "abc@example.com"

If I forget this, however, the commits will be seen as authored by my work account, which I don’t want. To automatically set this up, there’s two steps:

  1. Keep all the personal repositories in one folder, and in the root create a .gitconfig file containing the name and email you want

    [user]
email = abc@example.com
name = Drew Jose

  2. Add a conditional inclusion to the global git config. It includes a given .gitconfig file when git commands are run inside some directory. This should be after the globally defined [user] config, so that this takes precedence.

    [includeIf "gitdir:~/code/"]
path = ~/code/.gitconfig

This is quite neat and does what I want. One could extend this to add even more sorts of dynamic inclusions per folder.

entry.title: Development setup for three services with a database
entry.summary: Using tmux and scripting to set up a development environment for microservices locally.
entry.content:
At work, I have to develop a service that has an API server, a web server that serves UI, and a Slack bot. This uses a database. I can either run it locally via podman, or connect to one which already runs in a development cluster.

The web server requires the API server to provide some basic functionality, so even if I'm only developing the web service, I need both the API server and the database available, and vice versa.

Silly ’ol me was creating multiple tabs in my terminal, going to them manually, and running the setup commands via shell history. After the 90th time of doing this, I realised that I’m a programmer and such toil deserves to be scripted. So here we are.

Enter tmux

tmux, as many of you already know, is a terminal multiplexer, sort of a window manager for terminal processes. You can create a session and either interact with it by pressing key sequences from your keyboard, or you can send those key sequences from the terminal to automate some setup.

Here’s a script I created to set up all of the services.

Create a tmux session

#!/usr/bin/env zsh

WORK="$HOME/work" # Or wherever your WORK directory is

tmux kill-session -t devops-buddy
tmux new-session -d -s devops-buddy

We create a detached session with whatever name we want, and we kill a session with that name if it already exists. I don’t really care about persisting state manually because that’s what the database is for.

First service

# Pane 1: make watch
tmux send-keys "cd $WORK/backend" C-m
tmux send-keys "make watch" C-m

We cd to the repository of the first service and run whatever command we want. send-keys sends whatever text we enclose in quotes literally, and C-m means CTRL+m, which is the code for Enter. This actually executes the command. We can do it all in one line if we want but it looks cleaner this way.

Splitting the window and running the second process

tmux split-window -h -t 0 -c $WORK/frontend \; send-keys -t "$pane2" "npm run dev" C-m

You can split commands to tmux with an escaped semicolon: \;. split-window -h splits the window (tmux terminology for a single screen with multiple panes, sort of like a desktop) horizontally. The -c flag sents the current directory of the new pane, so we don’t have to execute cd manually. send-keys by default sends the keys to the active pane, which is, in this case, the newest one created.

Do this twice more

If you want to run four processes, you’d have to do the same thing again, twice, but with different arguments to split-window and send-keys

Attach to the session

tmux attach-session -t devops-buddy

This puts the tmux session in the foreground, split between your four panes. The good thing about this being a shell script is that you can do all sorts of setup interspersed with your tmux calls.

For instance, to connect to the database instance, I first connect to the kubernetes cluster it’s running in, and only then create the tmux pane that port-forwards to it.

How to use it

Just like a shell script! Since I’ve given all of the paths as absolute, I can run this script from any directory and get the same results. You can put something like this in your $PATH to not have to remember where you put it.

entry.content:
There's this podcaster in India known as BeerBiceps, his real name being Ranveer Allahbadia.
I've been a hater of his for a long time because of his cosying with the right-wing and penchant for saying things that don't make a lick of sense, without a hint of irony. The Prime Minister gave him some sort of national award in 2024.

Recently, he went on a game show with more annoying people as a judge, and asked a question to a contestant that went something like this:

Would you rather have to watch your parents have sex every day for the rest of your life, or join them once and stop it forever?

This has caused a huge uproar. Charges have been filed against everyone involved in the show. People want him to be jailed for some reason. Some are threatening him with violence over this1. He might be called to the parliament of the nation for this. You can read this article on "World Is One News", an international organisation that sometimes reports on India, to see just how many people have censured him: archived from WION.

While it is satisfying to see someone being treated horribly by the same oppressive forces they support, it's annoying to see just how regressive and angry so many people in India are. Nobody speaks up about how weird this is because they just don't care.

  1. I put this Times of India article into archive.is to prevent link rot, and it took ages to download everything due to how much cruft there is on the modern web :/ ↩

entry.title: Small server in python without dependencies
entry.summary: Code example using just built-ins for testing small proofs-of-concept
entry.content:
Python is a batteries-included kind of language, and so of course it comes with an HTTP server module. Today I wanted to have something small running on my computer without dependencies to test a server-side example, so I looked into how to create a minimal server using python built-ins. This is what I ended up with:

from http.server import *

class Resp(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.wfile.write(b"""HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Location: localhost:8000

<html>
<head><title>Hello, world</title></head>
<body>Minimal page written in python</body>
</html>
""")


def run(server_class=HTTPServer, handler_class=BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    server_address = ('', 8000)
    httpd = server_class(server_address, handler_class)
    httpd.serve_forever()

run(HTTPServer, Resp)

First of all, since this is just for trying it out, I imported everything from http.server. Never do this in normal code. We use HTTPServer and initialise it with the port we want to serve to and a handler class Resp that we subclass from BaseHTTPRequestHandler.

We add a do_GET method to our class, making it reply to all GET requests with that module. I don’t know how they implemented this, but it doesn’t sound like it would be pretty.

The request handler class has an instance variable wfile which is where we’re supposed to write our response. The response is supposed to be a bytestring, hence the b""", and it needs to be valid HTTP so that whatever tool we use to read it does not choke on it. Write the headers you want (including response code) and then the body.

There’s also a threading server you can use if you want concurrency, I’ve never tried it.

Extra info because I’m nice

Inside any directory with web files, you can run

python3 -m http.server 8000 # use the port you want

to serve the files to your browser. This is useful to get around restrictions that plain html files have when opened.

entry.title: Do not ask me to use Visual Studio Code or Chrome
entry.summary: I have been asked a couple times to switch from Emacs to VS Code or from Firefox/Safari to Chrome. Here’s why I will never do it.
entry.content:
I’m a software developer by profession, and most developers have settled on a couple of essential tools: VS Code for writing code, and the Chrome browser.

Obviously I have no problem with this; people can use the tools they want to (though the trillion-dollar corporations developing these tools do not have their best interests at heart), but some people do not abide by this rule and have told me to stop using the tools I want to use.

They have their reasons which make sense to them, the foremost being that everyone else uses Chrome/VS Code, and so using it will make sure I do not face weird issues, and that people looking at my screen actually have some idea of what’s going on.

Here are some reasons why I won’t ever switch to these tools:

  1. Chrome does not support a lot of useful extensions like uBlock origin (the Chrome store does list it but it is a hobbled version).
  2. They are not open source, which means that you are never sure what code you are running on your computer, and if there is a bug there is not a good way to look into it. Chrome and VS Code are “based on” open source projects called Chromium and Code - OSS, but these projects omit important functionality such as extensions.
  3. Chrome is effectively a monopoly, which causes web programmers to only test on Chrome to save on effort, making the web worse for everyone else (Safari, Firefox, Servo, etc.). If more people were to use these alternatives, it would stop the feedback loop of Chrome taking over the web because some sites just won’t work without it.
  4. VS Code and Chrome both send back usage data to their respective Trillion-dollar companies, which is a violation of privacy.
  5. I am quite happy using Emacs, and find it to be more featureful than VS Code. I can extend it easily using Emacs Lisp, and it is much smaller in size than VS Code (both in terms of size-on-disk and RAM usage), which means I can run it on any computer I want.
  6. VS Code is chiefly a marketing tool for Microsoft, and it allows them to get mindshare amongst developers. They also promote their own tools and cloud service within it. Emacs, developed by volunteers, does not want to sell me anything.

entry.title: Changed up my site's philosophy
entry.summary: I have decided to not package my site's theme to be reused by others anymore
entry.content:
Earlier, my site used to have two parts in my git forge; blog, and Solarized-Flex. “blog” contained just the text and the pelican config, while “Solarized-Flex” is my fork of another pelican theme with colours I like.

I noticed that the font files and css used by my site was much heavier than what I actually needed, as it used font-awesome, a big font with icons meant to be used as little images. My site only used four of them.

I kept them as-is though, in case someone else wanted to use my theme.

That's probably never going to happen, so now I have a much smaller site with all the extra bits removed; and just one git repository to deal with.

entry.title: Subsetting my fonts to speed up page loads
entry.summary: Removing unused fonts from my site to reduce its download size.
entry.content:
Subsetting a font means to remove all the characters you don’t actually use in order to reduce the size of the files. My site theme uses the font-awesome icon font, which maps code points to tiny images like the mastodon logo for example. I only use 4 of these, so the thousands of other icons is just unnecessary data that viewers have to download.

I will be using a js package called glyphhanger, which in turn uses the python library fonttools

  1. Use npm or pnpm to install glyphhanger globally: pnpm add -g glyphhanger or npm install -g glyphhanger
  2. Use pipx to install fonttools into its own virtual environment (you can install pipx via your package manager or via pip) pipx install fonttools
  3. Install compression libraries for use by glyphhanger into the fonttool environment: pipx inject fonttools zopfli brotli.
  4. Move to the directory with your fonts and execute: glyphhanger 'https://drewsh.com' --subset='*.ttf'. This will subset all fonts with the .ttf extension based on what is used in drewsh.com. You can also give a path to HTML files if you haven’t published the site yet.
  5. You will get a bunch of files ending with -subset and then the extension, which you can use in your site.

entry.title: Fauxspresso Lemonade
entry.summary: Something that tastes like espresso lemonade, but with less fancy ingredients
entry.content:
Okay, this is actually an aeropress limeade.
This is sort of a modified version of an aeropress recipe from Coffee with April

Ingredients

  • 13 grams coffee, medium roast
  • 130 ml water
  • Half a lime (15 grams)
  • Lots of ice (at least 40 grams)
  • Sugar/sweetener to taste

The lime variety I use is Key Lime, but any will do I suppose. I have made this with either a bit of maple syrup or artificial sweetener, you don't need a lot of it to make the drink taste good. If you don’t have an aeropress, 130ml of coffee in 1:10 ratio made with any method will work.

Steps

  1. Heat up 130 ml of water in a kettle to 100℃.

  2. Grind the coffee to a medium consistency, for reference it is 5 clicks on the Timemore Go.

  3. Pour in 50ml of the hot water in the aeropress, stir it a little bit and seal the aeropress so water doesn’t pass down (you do it by putting the plunger in a little bit and then pulling it almost all the way out to create pressure that prevents the water from leaving)

  4. After 30 seconds, put in the rest of the water (100ml), and wait for 90 seconds more.

  5. Pour the coffee out of the aeropress, and mix in your sweetener.

  6. Add the ice.

entry.title: Making the "compose" subcommand available to docker CLI in fish shell
entry.summary: Fish function example that allows you to use docker compose instead of docker-compose
entry.content:
Development tools today are very complicated to install and deal with, the foremost of which is the docker CLI. You install it via shell script on most systems and if you want docker compose, you need to install it separately. In some systems, it gets added as a subcommand, so that the docker binary can handle it, but on others you specifically have to call docker-compose, a single script, without spaces. If you try to run the compose subcommand in this case, docker will complain about it not being available.

The solution: using a fish function!

function docker -d "docker command with compose subcommand" -w docker
  if match "$argv[1]" "compose"
    docker-compose $argv[2..-1]
  else
    command docker $argv
  end
end

Save this in a file called docker.fish in your fish function directory (it’s in $XDG_CONFIG_DIR/fish/functions, or ~/.config/fish/functions).
-d gives the description of the function, and -w indicates that the function is wrapping the docker command, giving access to useful completions. The command fish built-in ensures that the function does not call itself, but rather the real docker binary.

Update:

Turns out all of this was unnecessary, and the only reason docker compose wasn't showing up as a subcommand is because it could not find the compose plugin

When you download docker-compose you might get this helpful tip

# Compose is a Docker plugin. For Docker to find the plugin, add "cliPluginsExtraDirs" to ~/.docker/config.json:
  "cliPluginsExtraDirs": [
      "/Users/arnavandrewjose/homebrew/lib/docker/cli-plugins"
  ]

entry.title: Things to do on an upcoming flight
entry.summary: Some things I can do that do not require an internet connection
entry.content:
I hate flying.

It's incredibly boring, the security circus is pointless and brings out the worst in co-passengers, more time is spent waiting for things to happen than actually being up in the air, and it's not great for the environment (though even if we were to stop taking flights, apparently just as many planes would take off).

I am also not used to being disconnected from the internet.

Here are some things I need to do, though, which can be easily accomplished during this great sinkhole of time.

  • Writing bindings for MelonJS for use with Hoot, a Wasm compiler for Guile Scheme. To write bindings, you need the API reference, which is available at https://melonjs.github.io/melonJS/. They do not make it easy to find and download any offline documentation, which is baffling, surely the docs exist somewhere before you bundle it into a website, why not make it available as text? Anyway, I found a tool called archivebox, which downloads a website with all linked assets as a bundle, so that should be good enough.
    Sidebar: Installing it on a 2015 MacBook Pro via Homebrew turned it into a furnace, probably because it installs node from source.
    Update from the next day: You need to clone the repo, install pnpm, and run pnpm install and then pnpm doc to have the docs show up in the melonjs/docs folder. Their logo isn't even a melon!
  • Continuing work on my C-based static-site generator (edit: I stopped work on it and nuked the codebase. maybe i'll do it in common lisp). This is not time-sensitive at all, but I find it quite fun and all I need to work on it is gdb and gcc.
  • Writing more of the Beginner Common Lisp book. I don't need to be connected to the internet for this, but Common List the Language, 2e by Guy Steele Jr. is a great reference for it so I have downloaded it.
